slides.heading: Hydrocarbons
slides.body_md: Part 1 — compounds of carbon and hydrogen only: alkanes (single bonds) and alkenes (a C=C double bond). Chapter 9 is taught for the school annual examination.

rows: Solvents and starting materials for dyes and drugs

visual.alt: Table of hydrocarbons met in daily life

slides.narration: Namaste! The gas in a kitchen cylinder, the petrol in a scooter, the polythene bag from the market and the flame of a welder are all hydrocarbons, compounds made of carbon and hydrogen only. In this chapter we meet four families. Part one covers alkanes and alkenes: how to name them, make them, and predict what they do when other reagents attack.

slides.heading: Families of hydrocarbons
slides.body_md: Hydrocarbons are classified as **saturated** (only single bonds) and **unsaturated** (C=C or C≡C), and as **open-chain or ring** (alicyclic and aromatic).

visual.alt: Table of the hydrocarbon families with general formula, hybridisation and shape

slides.narration: Hydrocarbons are sorted by the bonds between their carbon atoms. Alkanes have only single bonds, so every carbon is sp three hybridised and tetrahedral. Alkenes have a carbon carbon double bond, with sp two carbons that are flat. Alkynes have a triple bond and a straight sp carbon. Arenes contain the special ring of benzene. Remember the general formulas, because they tell you the degree of unsaturation.

slides.heading: Naming alkanes and chain isomerism
slides.body_md: Choose the **longest chain**, number from the end nearer the first branch, and list substituents **alphabetically**. Alkanes with four or more carbons show **chain isomerism**.

visual.alt: Table of the number of chain isomers of butane, pentane, hexane and heptane with an example

slides.narration: To name an alkane, find the longest continuous chain, number it from the end that gives the first branch the lowest number, and write the branches in alphabetical order. Because carbon atoms can be joined in different sequences, alkanes from four carbons upward show chain isomerism. Butane has two isomers, pentane three, hexane five and heptane nine. The count grows quickly with size.

slides.heading: Worked example: naming and counting isomers
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** (a) Name $\ce{(CH3)2CHCH2C(CH3)3}$. (b) Draw all chain isomers of $\ce{C5H12}$ and name them.

**(a)** Longest chain: five carbons (pentane). Methyl groups on C2, C2 and C4 when numbered from the end that gives the first branch the lower number: **2,2,4-trimethylpentane**.

**(b)** Pentane; 2-methylbutane; 2,2-dimethylpropane. Three isomers. The most branched has the lowest boiling point.

visual.alt: Flow for naming an alkane: longest chain, lowest locants, alphabetical order, locants and multiplying prefixes

slides.narration: Follow the steps in order. First find the longest chain, here five carbons, so the parent is pentane. Number it so the first branch gets the smaller number. Three methyl groups give the prefix trimethyl with locants two, two and four. For the isomer count, shorten the main chain one carbon at a time and move the branch around. Pentane gives exactly three isomers.

slides.heading: Preparation of alkanes
slides.body_md: **Hydrogenation** of alkenes or alkynes (Ni, Pt or Pd) and **reduction** of alkyl halides (Zn and acid) keep the carbon number. **Wurtz reaction** doubles the alkyl group; **decarboxylation** loses one carbon; **Kolbe electrolysis** joins two alkyl groups.

rows: Doubled, minus two carbons as CO₂

visual.alt: Table of five methods of preparing alkanes and the carbon count of the alkane

slides.narration: There are five routes to alkanes. Hydrogen adds across a double or triple bond over a nickel, platinum or palladium catalyst. A halide can be reduced by zinc and acid. In the Wurtz reaction sodium in dry ether joins two alkyl groups. Heating a sodium carboxylate with soda lime removes one carbon as carbonate. Electrolysing a carboxylate joins two alkyl groups at the anode. Watch how each method changes the carbon count.

slides.heading: Physical properties of alkanes
slides.body_md: Alkanes are **non-polar**: insoluble in water, soluble in non-polar solvents. Boiling point rises with chain length (stronger van der Waals forces) and **falls with branching** (smaller surface area). Methane to butane are gases at room temperature.

visual.alt: Table of boiling points of alkanes showing the rise with chain length and the fall with branching in the pentane isomers

slides.narration: Alkane molecules are non-polar, held together only by weak van der Waals forces. These grow with molecular size, so boiling points climb steadily from methane to octane. For isomers with the same mass, a branched molecule is more compact, touches its neighbours over a smaller area, and therefore boils lower. That is why the pentane isomers boil in the order shown in the table.

slides.heading: Chemical properties of alkanes
slides.body_md: Alkanes are fairly unreactive (strong, non-polar C–C and C–H bonds) but burn, and react under special conditions.

rows: Cu, 523 K, 100 atm; or Mn(II) ethanoate

visual.alt: Table of combustion, controlled oxidation, isomerisation, aromatisation and pyrolysis of alkanes

slides.narration: Alkanes burn completely to carbon dioxide and water, releasing a lot of heat, which is why they are fuels. With limited oxygen and a catalyst they give alcohols or acids. Aluminium chloride rearranges a straight chain into a branched one. Heated with metal oxides under pressure, hexane loses hydrogen and becomes benzene. At high temperature, big alkanes crack into smaller alkanes and alkenes.

slides.heading: Halogenation: a free-radical chain
slides.body_md: In sunlight, methane and chlorine give chloromethane. The mechanism has three stages: **initiation** (light splits Cl₂ into Cl• atoms), **propagation** (two steps that regenerate a radical), **termination** (radicals combine).

nodes.label: Initiation: Cl–Cl splits into two Cl•
Propagation 1: Cl• + CH₄ gives HCl + CH₃•
Propagation 2: CH₃• + Cl₂ gives CH₃Cl + Cl•
Termination: Cl• + Cl•, CH₃• + CH₃•, CH₃• + Cl•

visual.alt: Flow of the free-radical chain mechanism of chlorination of methane: initiation, two propagation steps that repeat, and termination

slides.narration: Chlorination of methane is a chain reaction. Ultraviolet light splits a chlorine molecule into two chlorine atoms, each with an unpaired electron. A chlorine atom pulls a hydrogen from methane, making hydrogen chloride and a methyl radical. The methyl radical then takes a chlorine atom from another chlorine molecule, producing chloromethane and a fresh chlorine atom, so the chain goes on until radicals meet and combine.

slides.heading: Conformations of ethane
slides.body_md: Rotation about the C–C single bond gives different spatial arrangements called **conformations**. The two extremes are **staggered** (dihedral angle 60°, lowest energy) and **eclipsed** (0°, highest energy), shown as Newman and sawhorse projections.

slides.narration: Because the sigma bond between the two carbons of ethane allows rotation, the hydrogens can take many relative positions. In a Newman projection we look straight down the carbon carbon bond. In the staggered form the back hydrogens sit midway between the front ones, as far apart as possible. In the eclipsed form they are exactly behind the front ones, so the electron clouds of the bonds repel more.

slides.heading: Energy and torsional strain
slides.body_md: Rotating one CH₃ group by 360° gives three energy maxima and three minima. The eclipsed form is about **12.5 kJ mol⁻¹** higher in energy than the staggered form (torsional strain), yet the barrier is small enough for rotation to be almost free at room temperature.

slides.narration: This graph plots the energy of ethane as one methyl group turns. Every sixty degrees the molecule swaps between a staggered minimum and an eclipsed maximum. The energy gap is about twelve point five kilojoules per mole, called torsional strain. Thermal energy at room temperature is only about two and a half kilojoules per mole, but molecules collide hard enough that the barrier is crossed countless times each second.

slides.heading: Worked example: how often is ethane eclipsed?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Estimate the ratio of molecules in one eclipsed conformation to one staggered conformation at 298 K, given a barrier of $12.5\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. ($R = 8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$; ignore entropy differences.)

**Step 1.** $RT = 8.314 \times 298 \approx 2478\ \text{J mol}^{-1} = 2.478\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

**Step 2.** Ratio $= e^{-12.5/2.478} = e^{-5.04}$.

**Step 3.** $e^{-5.04} \approx 6.4 \times 10^{-3}$: only about 6 eclipsed molecules for every 1000 staggered ones, so ethane spends almost all its time staggered.

slides.narration: We compare the barrier with the thermal energy. At room temperature, R times T is about two point five kilojoules per mole. The barrier is five times larger, so the fraction of molecules found at the top of the barrier is e to the power of minus five, about six in a thousand. Ethane therefore spends nearly all its time in the staggered form, although it keeps turning through every angle.

slides.heading: Alkenes: structure and geometric isomerism
slides.body_md: The C=C carbons are sp² hybridised; the double bond is one **σ** and one **π** bond (sideways overlap of p orbitals). The π bond prevents rotation, so alkenes with **two different groups on each double-bond carbon** show **cis–trans isomerism**.

slides.narration: In an alkene the two double bond carbons use sp two orbitals for sigma bonds, and the leftover p orbitals overlap sideways to form a pi bond. Breaking that overlap would need a lot of energy, so there is no free rotation. If each carbon holds two different groups, two arrangements are possible. The cis isomer has similar groups on the same side, the trans isomer on opposite sides. They differ in polarity, boiling point and melting point.

slides.heading: Preparation of alkenes
slides.body_md: **Partial reduction of alkynes:** Lindlar catalyst gives the **cis** alkene; sodium in liquid ammonia gives the **trans** alkene. **Dehydrohalogenation** (alcoholic KOH), **dehydration** of alcohols (conc. H₂SO₄) and **dehalogenation** of vicinal dihalides (Zn) also give alkenes.

visual.alt: Table of five methods of preparing alkenes with reagent and product

slides.narration: Alkenes can be made in several ways. Partial hydrogenation of an alkyne over a poisoned palladium catalyst, the Lindlar catalyst, stops at the cis alkene, while sodium in liquid ammonia gives the trans alkene. Alcoholic potassium hydroxide removes a hydrogen halide from a haloalkane. Concentrated sulfuric acid removes water from an alcohol. Zinc removes two halogens from a vicinal dihalide.

slides.heading: Markovnikov addition: the carbocation path
slides.body_md: Unsymmetrical alkene + HX: **H adds to the carbon with more hydrogens** (Markovnikov’s rule). The π bond attacks H⁺ in the slow step to give the **more stable carbocation** (3° > 2° > 1°), which is then trapped by X⁻.

Hydrogen could add to either carbon, but it goes to the end carbon, because that leaves the positive charge on the middle carbon, a secondary carbocation. Bromide then attacks it quickly, giving two bromopropane. That is Markovnikov addition.

slides.heading: Why the secondary carbocation wins

visual.caption: Schematic; the energies are not measured values.

slides.narration: The energy profile makes the point. Both routes begin at the same place, but the primary carbocation sits higher in energy, because it has only one alkyl group to share its positive charge. A higher intermediate goes with a higher transition state, so the primary route is slower. Nearly all the product therefore comes through the secondary carbocation, which is the Markovnikov rule explained.

slides.heading: Quick check: carbocation stability
slides.body_md: Rank carbocations or predict the Markovnikov product of a substituted alkene.
slides.narration: Quick check. Count the alkyl groups on the positively charged carbon.

slides.heading: Peroxide effect and other additions
slides.body_md: With **HBr only**, in the presence of a peroxide, addition is **anti-Markovnikov** by a free-radical chain (Kharasch effect): Br• adds first to give the more stable 2° radical. HCl and HI do not show it. Other additions: H₂ (Ni) gives alkanes; Br₂ in CCl₄ gives vicinal dibromides (red-brown colour disappears); H₂O with H⁺ follows Markovnikov.

visual.alt: Table of additions to alkenes including the peroxide effect that occurs only with hydrogen bromide

slides.narration: Peroxides change the course of hydrogen bromide addition, but only hydrogen bromide. A peroxide makes bromine atoms, and a bromine atom adds to the end carbon of the alkene, because that gives the more stable secondary radical. The radical then takes a hydrogen from hydrogen bromide. The result is anti Markovnikov. With hydrogen chloride or hydrogen iodide the chain steps are not favourable, so the usual product forms.

slides.heading: Ozonolysis, Baeyer’s test and polymerisation
slides.body_md: **Ozonolysis** (O₃, then Zn and water) cuts the C=C bond and puts C=O on each carbon; the products tell you where the double bond was. **Baeyer’s test:** cold dilute alkaline KMnO₄ is decolourised and a vicinal diol forms. **Polymerisation:** many ethene molecules join to give polythene.

visual.alt: Table showing the carbonyl compound formed from each type of double-bond carbon in ozonolysis

slides.narration: Three more reactions complete the picture. In ozonolysis, ozone cuts the double bond and each carbon becomes a carbonyl carbon. A carbon with two hydrogens gives methanal, one with a single alkyl group gives an aldehyde, and one with two alkyl groups gives a ketone. In the Baeyer test, purple permanganate turns brown as a diol forms. Finally, ethene molecules join in long chains to make polythene.

slides.heading: Worked example: identify the alkene
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** An alkene $\ce{C6H12}$ on ozonolysis (Zn, H₂O) gives only propanone. Identify it and check the formula.

**Step 1.** One product only, so the alkene is symmetrical: both carbons of C=C become $\ce{(CH3)2C=O}$.

**Step 2.** Join the two carbons: $\ce{(CH3)2C=C(CH3)2}$, **2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene**.

**Step 3.** Check: two $\ce{C3H6O}$ units give $\ce{C6H12}$ once the two oxygens are removed. ✓

headers: Carbon that was in the C=C

visual.alt: Table showing two propanone molecules each contributing a dimethyl-substituted double-bond carbon

slides.narration: To work backwards from ozonolysis products, remove the oxygen from each carbonyl and join the two carbons with a double bond. Here both fragments are propanone, so the alkene is symmetrical, with two methyl groups on each carbon: two three dimethylbut two ene. Check by adding the carbons: three plus three is six, and the hydrogens are six plus six, twelve. The formula agrees.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂: made by hydrogenation, Wurtz, decarboxylation, Kolbe; react by free-radical halogenation, combustion, isomerisation, aromatisation, cracking.

Alkenes CₙH₂ₙ: sp², π bond, cis–trans isomerism; Lindlar gives cis, Na/NH₃ gives trans.
Markovnikov via the more stable carbocation; peroxide effect for HBr only.
Ozonolysis locates the double bond; Baeyer’s test detects it.

visual.alt: Table comparing the behaviour of alkanes and alkenes towards four reagents

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part one. Alkanes are saturated and give substitution through free radicals. Ethane has staggered and eclipsed conformations separated by about twelve point five kilojoules per mole. Alkenes have a pi bond, show cis trans isomerism, and add reagents. Hydrogen halides add by Markovnikov’s rule through the more stable carbocation, except hydrogen bromide with peroxide. Ozonolysis tells us where the double bond was.

slides.heading: Alkynes and Aromatic Hydrocarbons
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the carbon–carbon triple bond and the special stability of benzene.

rows: Starting material for plastics and dyes; a toxic solvent

visual.alt: Table of an alkyne and aromatic hydrocarbons and their uses

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Ethyne burns with a flame hot enough to cut steel, and benzene is the parent of thousands of dyes, drugs and plastics. Yet benzene does not behave like an alkene, even though it looks as if it has three double bonds. We shall see why, and we shall learn how benzene reacts, where new groups enter the ring, and why some aromatic compounds are dangerous.

slides.heading: Alkynes: structure
slides.body_md: In ethyne the carbons are **sp hybridised**: linear, 180°, one σ and two π bonds. The C≡C bond is short and strong.

visual.alt: Table comparing bond length, enthalpy, hybridisation and s-character of ethane, ethene and ethyne carbon bonds

slides.narration: In ethyne each carbon uses one s and one p orbital to make two sp hybrid orbitals, giving a straight molecule. The two leftover p orbitals on each carbon form two pi bonds. The triple bond is the shortest and strongest carbon carbon bond we meet. Notice the s character: it rises from twenty five to fifty percent as we go from alkane to alkyne, and this explains the acidity of ethyne.

slides.heading: Acidity of terminal alkynes
slides.body_md: An sp carbon holds its electrons closer to the nucleus (50% s-character), so it is more electronegative and the ≡C–H hydrogen is **weakly acidic**. Order of acidity: **ethyne > ethene > ethane**. Only **terminal** alkynes react with sodium or sodium amide.

visual.alt: Table of acidity of ethyne, ethene and ethane and which react with sodium or sodium amide

slides.narration: Why is ethyne a weak acid while ethane is not? The answer is the hybridisation of the carbon holding the hydrogen. An sp carbon has half s character, so it pulls electrons more strongly, stabilises the negative charge left after a proton is lost, and releases hydrogen more easily. Sodium releases hydrogen gas, and sodium amide removes the proton to give ammonia. A hydrocarbon like but two yne has no such hydrogen, so it does not react.

slides.heading: Quick check: terminal alkynes
slides.body_md: Decide which alkyne reacts with sodium.
slides.narration: Quick check. Look for a hydrogen attached directly to a triple-bonded carbon.

slides.heading: Preparation of alkynes
slides.body_md: Ethyne is made in the laboratory from **calcium carbide** and water. Alkynes in general are made by **double dehydrohalogenation of a vicinal (or geminal) dihalide** with a strong base.

edges.label: second KOH or NaNH₂: lose HBr

visual.alt: Flow of double dehydrohalogenation of a vicinal dibromide through a vinyl bromide to an alkyne

slides.narration: Calcium carbide reacts with water at once, giving ethyne gas and calcium hydroxide, the old carbide lamp reaction. For other alkynes we start from a dihalide with halogens on neighbouring carbons. Alcoholic potassium hydroxide removes one molecule of hydrogen bromide to give a vinyl bromide, and a second removal, often with sodium amide, gives the triple bond.

slides.heading: Addition reactions of alkynes
slides.body_md: Alkynes add two molecules of H₂, X₂ or HX. **H₂:** Ni gives the alkane; Lindlar gives the **cis** alkene; Na/liquid NH₃ gives the **trans** alkene. **HX** adds by Markovnikov’s rule, twice. **Water** (HgSO₄, dilute H₂SO₄) gives a carbonyl compound by tautomerism.

visual.alt: Table of products of addition reactions of ethyne and propyne

slides.narration: Alkynes add reagents twice, because they have two pi bonds. Bromine in excess gives a tetrabromo compound. Hydrogen bromide adds twice by Markovnikov’s rule, putting both bromines on the same carbon. In the presence of mercury salts and dilute acid, water adds to ethyne to give an unstable enol that shifts at once to ethanal; propyne similarly gives propanone.

slides.heading: Worked example: predict the products
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Write the product of (a) but-2-yne with H₂/Lindlar, (b) but-2-yne with Na/liquid NH₃, (c) propyne with excess HBr, (d) ethyne with Na.

**(a)** cis-But-2-ene. **(b)** trans-But-2-ene.

**(c)** Markovnikov twice: $\ce{CH3CBr2CH3}$, 2,2-dibromopropane.

**(d)** $\ce{CH#CNa}$ (sodium ethynide) and hydrogen gas.

visual.alt: Flow for predicting the reaction of an alkyne from the reagent: acid-base, partial reduction or HX addition

slides.narration: First look at the reagent. Sodium or sodium amide acts as a base, and only a terminal alkyne has a hydrogen to give up. Hydrogen with Lindlar catalyst stops at the cis alkene, while sodium in liquid ammonia gives the trans alkene. Hydrogen halides add twice, always following Markovnikov, so propyne ends as two two dibromopropane with both bromines on the middle carbon.

slides.heading: Cyclic polymerisation and combustion
slides.body_md: Ethyne passed through a **red-hot iron tube (873 K)** trimerises to **benzene**. Ethyne burns with a sooty, very hot flame (oxy-acetylene torch).

rows: CO₂ + H₂O, flame about 3000 K with pure oxygen

visual.alt: Table of the cyclic polymerisation and combustion of ethyne

slides.narration: Here is a surprising reaction. Pass ethyne through a red hot iron tube and three molecules join in a ring to give benzene. This is called cyclic polymerisation. Ethyne also burns in oxygen with an extremely hot flame, which is why the oxyacetylene torch can cut and weld metal. In air it burns with a smoky flame because the carbon content is high.

slides.narration: Benzene puzzled chemists for decades. It has six carbons and six hydrogens, yet it does not decolourise bromine water or permanganate as alkenes do. Experiments show all carbon carbon bonds are the same length, one hundred and thirty nine picometres. Neither Kekulé structure alone can account for that. The real molecule is a resonance hybrid, a blend of both, shown by a hexagon with a circle.

slides.narration: Each carbon of benzene uses sp two orbitals to bond to two neighbours and one hydrogen, so the ring is flat with angles of one hundred and twenty degrees. The leftover p orbitals stand upright and overlap sideways with both neighbours, forming a continuous doughnut of electron density above and below the plane. Six electrons are shared by all six carbons, and this delocalisation lowers the energy of benzene.

slides.heading: Resonance energy: how stable is benzene?
slides.body_md: Hydrogenation of cyclohexene releases about $120\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Three isolated double bonds would release $3 \times 120 = 360$, but benzene releases only about $208\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. The difference, about **150 kJ mol⁻¹**, is the **resonance (delocalisation) energy**.

visual.alt: Table of heats of hydrogenation of cyclohexene, the expected value for three double bonds, and benzene, giving the resonance energy

slides.narration: We can measure the stability of benzene. Adding hydrogen to one double bond in cyclohexene gives out about one hundred and twenty kilojoules per mole. Three double bonds should give out three hundred and sixty, but benzene gives out only about two hundred and eight. Benzene is therefore about one hundred and fifty kilojoules per mole more stable than expected. This is why benzene prefers substitution, which keeps the ring, to addition.

slides.heading: Aromaticity and the Hückel rule
slides.body_md: A compound is **aromatic** if its ring is **planar, cyclic, fully conjugated** and has **(4n + 2) π electrons** (n = 0, 1, 2 …): 2, 6, 10, 14 …

visual.alt: Table applying the Hückel rule to benzene, naphthalene, anthracene, cyclobutadiene and cyclooctatetraene

slides.narration: The Hückel rule tells us when a ring is aromatic. The molecule must be flat, cyclic, and conjugated all the way round, and the number of pi electrons must equal four n plus two, where n is zero or a whole number. Benzene has six, naphthalene ten, anthracene fourteen, all of the form. Cyclobutadiene has four, and cyclooctatetraene has eight and is tub shaped, so neither is aromatic.

slides.heading: Quick check: Hückel rule
slides.body_md: Apply the 4n + 2 rule.
slides.narration: Quick check. Count the pi electrons and test whether the number fits four n plus two.

slides.heading: Preparation of benzene
slides.body_md: Benzene is obtained industrially from coal tar and petroleum (aromatisation). In the laboratory: **cyclic polymerisation of ethyne**, **decarboxylation of sodium benzoate** with soda lime, and **reduction of phenol** with zinc dust.

visual.alt: Table of four methods of preparing benzene

slides.narration: Benzene is made on a large scale from coal tar and from petroleum. In the laboratory, ethyne trimerises in a hot iron tube. Heating sodium benzoate with soda lime removes the carboxyl group as carbonate and leaves benzene. Phenol heated with zinc dust loses its oxygen to the zinc, again leaving benzene. Hexane can also be converted to benzene with metal oxide catalysts.

slides.heading: Electrophiles for substitution
slides.body_md: Because of its π cloud, benzene reacts with **electrophiles** (E⁺) and keeps its ring: **electrophilic substitution**. The electrophile is generated in each reaction.

rows: Cl₂ or Br₂ + anhydrous FeCl₃ or FeBr₃

slides.narration: The pi cloud of benzene attracts electron poor species called electrophiles. In each reaction the electrophile must first be made. A mixture of nitric and sulfuric acids makes the nitronium ion. Chlorine with iron chloride gives a strongly polarised chlorine. Sulfur trioxide in fuming sulfuric acid does the sulfonation. And an alkyl or acyl chloride with aluminium chloride gives a carbocation or an acylium ion for the Friedel Crafts reactions.

slides.body_md: Step 1 (slow): the π electrons attack E⁺ to form the **arenium ion** (σ complex), a resonance-stabilised carbocation. Step 2 (fast): loss of H⁺ **restores the aromatic ring**.

slides.narration: All the substitution reactions follow one pattern. In the slow first step, two electrons from the pi cloud form a bond to the electrophile. This gives the arenium ion, in which one carbon holds both the hydrogen and the new group, and the positive charge is shared by the other five. In the fast second step a proton leaves, the electrons return to the ring, and aromaticity is restored.

slides.heading: Worked example: two substitutions
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Write the equation and electrophile for (a) nitration of benzene, (b) Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene with ethanoyl chloride.

**(a)** $\ce{C6H6 + HNO3 ->[conc. H2SO4, 333 K] C6H5NO2 + H2O}$; electrophile $\ce{NO2+}$.

**(b)** $\ce{C6H6 + CH3COCl ->[anhyd. AlCl3] C6H5COCH3 + HCl}$; electrophile $\ce{CH3CO+}$. The product is phenylethanone (acetophenone).

visual.alt: Flow of electrophilic substitution: generate the electrophile, attack by the pi cloud, arenium ion, loss of proton

slides.narration: In every case, name the electrophile first. For nitration, concentrated nitric acid and sulfuric acid at about fifty degrees give nitrobenzene and water. For acylation, ethanoyl chloride with anhydrous aluminium chloride supplies the acylium ion, and benzene is converted into phenylethanone, with hydrogen chloride as the by product. The aluminium chloride must be anhydrous, because water destroys it.

slides.heading: Directive influence of substituents
slides.body_md: A group already on the ring decides **where** the next group goes and **how fast**. **Activating, o/p-directing:** –OH, –NH₂, –OCH₃, –CH₃ (electron-donating). **Deactivating, o/p-directing:** halogens. **Deactivating, m-directing:** –NO₂, –CN, –CHO, –COOH, –SO₃H (electron-withdrawing).

rows: Lone pair donated into the ring (+M)
–M and –I withdraw electrons, most from o and p

visual.alt: Table of directing effects of substituents on benzene with the effect on rate, orientation and reason

slides.narration: A substituent controls both the speed of further substitution and the position. Groups that push electrons into the ring, such as hydroxyl, amino and methyl, make it more reactive and direct the newcomer to the ortho and para positions. Groups that pull electrons out, such as nitro, cyano, aldehyde and carboxyl, make the ring less reactive and send the newcomer to the meta position. Halogens are the odd ones: deactivating but ortho and para directing.

slides.body_md: Predict the position of substitution.
slides.narration: Quick check. Decide whether the group donates or withdraws electrons.

slides.heading: Worked example: reading isomer data
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Nitration of methylbenzene gives 58% ortho, 4% meta and 38% para products (approximate). Calculate the yield per position and explain.

**Per position:** ortho $= 58 \div 2 = 29$, meta $= 4 \div 2 = 2$, para $= 38 \div 1 = 38$.

**Explanation.** The CH₃ group donates electrons (+I, hyperconjugation), stabilising the arenium ions from ortho and para attack, where the positive charge falls on the carbon bearing CH₃. Para is favoured over ortho for steric reasons.

visual.alt: Table of the nitration yield of methylbenzene per ortho, meta and para position

slides.narration: Data on isomer ratios need care, because there are two ortho positions, two meta positions and only one para position. Dividing the totals by the number of positions shows that each para position is the most reactive, each ortho position next, and each meta position is almost unreactive. The methyl group donates electrons and stabilises the arenium ion when the charge falls next to it, which happens only for ortho and para attack.

slides.heading: Carcinogenicity and toxicity
slides.body_md: **Benzene** is toxic: long exposure damages bone marrow and can cause leukaemia. **Polynuclear (fused-ring) hydrocarbons** with more than two benzene rings, such as **benzpyrene** (C₂₀H₁₂), are carcinogenic. They form by incomplete combustion of coal, petroleum and tobacco and damage DNA.

rows: Tobacco smoke, charred food, coal and vehicle exhaust

visual.alt: Table of benzene, naphthalene and benzpyrene with source and hazard

slides.narration: Aromatic compounds are not harmless. Benzene vapour, breathed over years, damages the bone marrow and can cause leukaemia, so it is no longer used as an ordinary solvent. Compounds with several fused benzene rings, such as benzpyrene, form when coal, petrol, wood or tobacco burn incompletely. In the body they are converted into reactive products that damage DNA and may cause cancer. Good ventilation and clean combustion lower the risk.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Alkynes: sp, linear; terminal ≡C–H is acidic (sp, 50% s); CaC₂ gives ethyne; two additions; ethyne gives benzene on cyclic polymerisation.
Benzene: planar, C–C 139 pm, resonance hybrid, resonance energy about 150 kJ mol⁻¹.
Aromatic: planar, cyclic, conjugated, (4n + 2) π electrons.
Electrophilic substitution: nitration, halogenation, sulfonation, Friedel–Crafts alkylation and acylation, via the arenium ion.
Activating groups: o/p; deactivating groups: m (halogens: o/p).
Polynuclear hydrocarbons such as benzpyrene are carcinogenic.

visual.alt: Summary table of electrophilic substitution reactions of benzene

slides.narration: To sum up Part two. Alkynes have an acidic terminal hydrogen, add reagents twice, and ethyne trimerises to benzene. Benzene is a flat resonance hybrid with a delocalised six electron cloud, and it obeys the Hückel rule. It undergoes electrophilic substitution through the arenium ion. Substituents direct the next group to ortho and para or to meta. And fused ring hydrocarbons like benzpyrene are carcinogenic.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Only terminal alkynes react with Na, NaNH₂ and ammoniacal silver nitrate.
Write the electrophile and its generation in every substitution answer.
In a Hückel question, check planarity and conjugation before counting electrons.
Halogens: deactivating but ortho and para directing; nitro: meta.
Friedel–Crafts fails on strongly deactivated rings such as nitrobenzene; use anhydrous AlCl₃.

rows: Methyl is ortho and para directing

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 2 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some last tips. Write the electrophile and how it forms every time you answer a substitution question. For Hückel, check that the ring is flat and fully conjugated before counting electrons. Remember the odd case of halogens, which are deactivating yet ortho and para directing. And remember that nitrobenzene is too deactivated for a Friedel Crafts reaction, so aluminium chloride cannot help it.

sections.heading: 1. Alkanes: nomenclature, isomerism and preparation
sections.body_md:
**General formula** $\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n+2}$; sp³ carbons, tetrahedral, C–C 154 pm. **Naming:** longest chain, lowest locants for the first branch, substituents alphabetical (2,2,4-trimethylpentane). **Chain isomers:** C₄H₁₀ 2, C₅H₁₂ 3, C₆H₁₄ 5, C₇H₁₆ 9.

**Preparation:**
- Hydrogenation of alkenes or alkynes (Ni, Pt or Pd): same carbon number.
- Reduction of alkyl halides: $\ce{C2H5Cl + Zn + HCl -> C2H6 + ZnCl2}$.
- **Wurtz:** $\ce{2CH3Br + 2Na ->[dry ether] C2H6 + 2NaBr}$ (a mixture of alkyl halides gives a mixture of alkanes).
- **Decarboxylation:** $\ce{CH3COONa + NaOH ->[CaO, heat] CH4 + Na2CO3}$ (one carbon less).
- **Kolbe electrolysis:** $\ce{2CH3COONa + 2H2O -> C2H6 + 2CO2 + H2 + 2NaOH}$ (R–R at the anode).

key_terms.definition_md: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different carbon skeletons.
Coupling of two alkyl halide molecules by sodium in dry ether to give an alkane with twice the carbons.
Electrolysis of an aqueous sodium or potassium carboxylate to give an alkane R–R at the anode.

sections.heading: 2. Alkanes: properties and conformations of ethane
sections.body_md:
**Physical:** non-polar; boiling point rises with chain length and falls with branching (pentane 309 K, 2-methylbutane 301 K, 2,2-dimethylpropane 283 K).

**Chemical:** combustion; controlled oxidation (CH₄ → CH₃OH with Cu, 523 K, 100 atm; ethane → ethanoic acid with Mn(II) ethanoate); isomerisation (AlCl₃/HCl); aromatisation (hexane → benzene, Cr₂O₃/V₂O₅, 773 K); pyrolysis (cracking). **Halogenation** is a free-radical chain: initiation (Cl₂ → 2Cl•), propagation (Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + CH₃•; CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•), termination (radical + radical). Rates of H abstraction: 3° > 2° > 1°; F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.

**Conformations of ethane:** staggered (dihedral angle 60°, minimum) and eclipsed (0°, maximum). The eclipsed form is about **12.5 kJ mol⁻¹** higher (torsional strain, about 4 kJ mol⁻¹ per eclipsed H–H pair), but rotation is nearly free at room temperature.

key_terms.definition_md: A species with an unpaired electron, formed by homolytic fission.
Ethane conformation with the hydrogens of one carbon midway between those of the other; lowest energy.
Extra energy of the eclipsed conformation caused by repulsion between electron clouds of eclipsed bonds.

sections.heading: 3. Alkenes: structure, geometric isomerism and preparation
sections.body_md:
**General formula** $\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n}$; sp² carbons, planar, 120°, C=C 134 pm; one σ and one π bond (restricted rotation). **Geometric (cis–trans) isomerism** needs two different groups on each C of C=C: cis-but-2-ene (bp 277 K, mp 134 K, polar) and trans-but-2-ene (bp 274 K, mp 168 K, non-polar, packs better).

**Preparation:** partial reduction of alkynes (Lindlar → cis; Na/liquid NH₃ → trans); dehydrohalogenation (alcoholic KOH); dehydration of alcohols (conc. H₂SO₄, 443 K); dehalogenation of vicinal dihalides (Zn).

key_terms.definition_md: Stereoisomers differing in the arrangement of groups about a double bond (or ring).
Palladium on calcium carbonate poisoned with quinoline; stops alkyne hydrogenation at the cis alkene.

sections.heading: 4. Alkenes: reactions
sections.body_md:
**Addition:** H₂ (Ni) → alkane; X₂ → vicinal dihalide (bromine in CCl₄ decolourised); HX and H₂O (H⁺) follow **Markovnikov's rule**: H adds to the carbon with more H. The π bond attacks H⁺ to give the more stable carbocation (3° > 2° > 1°), then X⁻ attacks.

**Peroxide (Kharasch) effect:** with peroxide, **HBr only** adds anti-Markovnikov through a radical chain (Br• adds to give the more stable radical): but-1-ene → 1-bromobutane.

**Ozonolysis** (O₃, then Zn/H₂O): C=C is cut and each carbon becomes C=O: =CH₂ → HCHO, =CHR → RCHO, =CR₂ → R₂C=O. **Baeyer's test:** cold dilute alkaline KMnO₄ is decolourised (brown MnO₂), vicinal diol formed. **Polymerisation:** n CH₂=CH₂ → polythene.

key_terms.definition_md: In the addition of HX to an unsymmetrical alkene, hydrogen adds to the carbon that already has more hydrogens.
Anti-Markovnikov addition of HBr in the presence of peroxides.
Cleavage of C=C by ozone followed by reductive work-up, giving aldehydes and ketones.

sections.heading: 5. Alkynes
sections.body_md:
**General formula** $\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n-2}$; sp carbons, linear, C≡C 120 pm. **Acidity:** sp carbon (50% s-character) is more electronegative, so terminal alkynes are weakly acidic: ethyne > ethene > ethane. $\ce{2CH#CH + 2Na -> 2CH#CNa + H2}$; $\ce{CH#CH + NaNH2 -> CH#CNa + NH3}$.

**Preparation:** $\ce{CaC2 + 2H2O -> C2H2 + Ca(OH)2}$; vicinal dihalide + alcoholic KOH (twice).

**Addition:** H₂ (Ni → alkane; Lindlar → cis; Na/NH₃ → trans); X₂ (twice); HX (Markovnikov, twice); H₂O/HgSO₄/H₂SO₄ → ethanal from ethyne, propanone from propyne.

**Cyclic polymerisation:** $\ce{3C2H2 ->[873 K] C6H6}$.

sections.heading: 6. Benzene: structure, resonance and aromaticity
sections.body_md:
Benzene $\ce{C6H6}$: planar regular hexagon, all C–C 139 pm, bond angles 120°. **Resonance hybrid** of two Kekulé structures; delocalised π cloud of six electrons above and below the plane. **Resonance energy** about 150 kJ mol⁻¹ (hydrogenation: −208 observed against −360 expected for three C=C). Benzene prefers substitution to addition.

**Aromaticity (Hückel):** planar, cyclic, fully conjugated, (4n + 2) π electrons: benzene 6, naphthalene 10, anthracene 14. Cyclobutadiene (4) and cyclooctatetraene (8, tub-shaped) are not aromatic.

**Preparation:** cyclic polymerisation of ethyne; $\ce{C6H5COONa + NaOH ->[CaO, heat] C6H6 + Na2CO3}$; $\ce{C6H5OH + Zn -> C6H6 + ZnO}$; aromatisation of hexane.

key_terms.definition_md: The real structure of a molecule that is represented by two or more contributing structures.
A planar, cyclic, fully conjugated compound with (4n + 2) π electrons.
The extra stability of a molecule compared with its most stable single contributing structure.

sections.heading: 7. Electrophilic substitution, directing effects and toxicity
sections.body_md:
**Mechanism:** E⁺ is attacked by the π cloud (slow) to give the arenium ion; loss of H⁺ (fast) restores the ring.

**Reactions:** nitration (conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄, 333 K; NO₂⁺); halogenation (X₂, FeX₃); sulfonation (fuming H₂SO₄; SO₃); Friedel–Crafts alkylation (RCl, anhydrous AlCl₃) and acylation (RCOCl, anhydrous AlCl₃, giving an aryl ketone). Friedel–Crafts fails on strongly deactivated rings such as nitrobenzene.

**Directing effects:** –OH, –NH₂, –OCH₃, –CH₃ activate and direct o/p; –Cl, –Br deactivate but direct o/p; –NO₂, –CN, –CHO, –COOH, –SO₃H deactivate and direct m.

**Toxicity:** benzene harms bone marrow; polynuclear hydrocarbons such as **benzpyrene** (formed by incomplete combustion of coal, petroleum and tobacco) are **carcinogenic** because they damage DNA.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving the peroxide effect for HCl or HI (it is for HBr only).
- Writing H adding to the carbon with fewer hydrogens in Markovnikov addition.
- Drawing the Newman projection without the circle for the back carbon, or calling the eclipsed form the more stable one.
- Calling cyclooctatetraene or cyclobutadiene aromatic.
- Writing the product of Friedel–Crafts acylation as an alkylbenzene.
- Forgetting that only terminal alkynes react with sodium.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: product, reagent, name or classification.
- Mechanism answers: electrophile or radical generated (1), slow step with intermediate (1), product (1).
- Prediction (2 marks): rule named (1) + product (1).
- Ozonolysis: carbonyl products (1) + alkene structure (1).

cards.front_md: General formulas of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes?
cards.back_md: $\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n+2}$, $\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n}$, $\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n-2}$.

cards.front_md: How many chain isomers has C₅H₁₂?
cards.back_md: Three: pentane, 2-methylbutane, 2,2-dimethylpropane.

cards.front_md: Wurtz reaction?
cards.back_md: Alkyl halide + Na in dry ether gives an alkane with twice the carbons: 2RX + 2Na → R–R + 2NaX.

cards.front_md: Effect of decarboxylation on carbon number?
cards.back_md: The alkane has one carbon less than the sodium carboxylate (soda lime, heat).

cards.front_md: Kolbe electrolysis product at the anode?
cards.back_md: R–R (an alkane with twice the carbons of R), plus CO₂.

cards.front_md: Why does branching lower the boiling point?
cards.back_md: Smaller surface area of contact, weaker van der Waals forces.

cards.front_md: Initiation step in chlorination of methane?
cards.back_md: Light splits Cl₂ into two chlorine radicals (Cl•).

cards.front_md: Two propagation steps of methane chlorination?
cards.back_md: Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + CH₃•; CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•.

cards.front_md: Order of ease of H abstraction by a radical?
cards.back_md: 3° > 2° > 1° (more stable radical).

cards.front_md: Catalyst and product for aromatisation of hexane?
cards.back_md: Cr₂O₃/V₂O₅/Mo₂O₃, 773 K, 10–20 atm gives benzene and H₂.

cards.front_md: Draw the staggered Newman projection of ethane.
cards.back_md: Circle for back carbon; front bonds meet at the centre at 120°; back bonds start at the circle midway between them (dihedral 60°).

cards.front_md: Which ethane conformation is more stable and by how much?
cards.back_md: Staggered, by about 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹ (torsional strain of the eclipsed form).

cards.front_md: Why is rotation about C–C in ethane almost free at 298 K?
cards.back_md: The barrier (12.5 kJ mol⁻¹) is small compared with collision energies; about 6 in 1000 molecules are eclipsed at any moment.

cards.front_md: Geometry and bonding of the C=C carbons?
cards.back_md: sp², trigonal planar (120°), one σ and one π bond.

cards.front_md: Condition for cis–trans isomerism in an alkene?
cards.back_md: Two different groups on each carbon of C=C, and restricted rotation about the π bond.

cards.front_md: Which but-2-ene isomer has the higher melting point?
cards.back_md: trans (symmetrical, packs better): 168 K against 134 K for cis.

cards.front_md: Lindlar catalyst gives which alkene?
cards.back_md: The cis alkene (Pd/CaCO₃ poisoned with quinoline).

cards.front_md: Na in liquid NH₃ reduces an alkyne to?
cards.back_md: The trans alkene.

cards.front_md: State Markovnikov’s rule.
cards.back_md: In HX addition to an unsymmetrical alkene, H adds to the carbon with more hydrogens (X goes to the carbon with fewer).

cards.front_md: Order of carbocation stability?
cards.back_md: 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃⁺ (hyperconjugation and +I effect of alkyl groups).

cards.front_md: The peroxide effect: which reagent?
cards.back_md: HBr only (not HCl or HI); gives anti-Markovnikov product via radicals.

cards.front_md: Ozonolysis products from =CH₂, =CHR and =CR₂ carbons?
cards.back_md: Methanal, an aldehyde and a ketone respectively.

cards.front_md: Baeyer’s test observation?
cards.back_md: Cold dilute alkaline KMnO₄ is decolourised (brown MnO₂); a vicinal diol forms.

cards.front_md: Why is ethyne more acidic than ethene or ethane?
cards.back_md: The sp carbon (50% s-character) is more electronegative and stabilises the anion.

cards.front_md: Laboratory preparation of ethyne?
cards.back_md: $\ce{CaC2 + 2H2O -> C2H2 + Ca(OH)2}$.

cards.front_md: Product of hydration of ethyne and of propyne?
cards.back_md: Ethanal and propanone (via enol–keto tautomerism).

cards.front_md: What does red-hot iron do to ethyne?
cards.back_md: Cyclic polymerisation: three C₂H₂ give C₆H₆ (benzene) at 873 K.

cards.front_md: C–C bond length in benzene?
cards.back_md: 139 pm, between C–C (154 pm) and C=C (134 pm).

cards.front_md: State the Hückel rule.
cards.back_md: A planar, cyclic, fully conjugated ring is aromatic if it has (4n + 2) π electrons.

cards.front_md: Electrophile in nitration, and in Friedel–Crafts acylation?
cards.back_md: NO₂⁺ (nitronium ion); RCO⁺ (acylium ion).

cards.front_md: Which groups are m-directing?
cards.back_md: –NO₂, –CN, –CHO, –COOH, –SO₃H (electron-withdrawing).

cards.back_md: Fused-ring compounds like benzpyrene (from incomplete combustion) damage DNA and are carcinogenic.

questions.stem_md: The IUPAC name of $\ce{(CH3)2CHCH(CH2CH3)2}$ is:
questions.solution_md: Two five-carbon chains are possible; the one carrying two substituents (methyl and ethyl) is chosen, and numbering from the methyl end gives the locants 2 and 3. Substituents are listed alphabetically, ethyl before methyl: 3-ethyl-2-methylpentane — option (a). Option (d) has the substituents out of alphabetical order.

questions.stem_md: How many chain isomers (including the straight-chain compound) has hexane, $\ce{C6H14}$?
questions.solution_md: Hexane, 2-methylpentane, 3-methylpentane, 2,2-dimethylbutane and 2,3-dimethylbutane: five isomers — option (d).

questions.stem_md: 2-Bromobutane is warmed with sodium metal in dry ether. The alkane formed is:
questions.solution_md: Two $\ce{CH3CH2CH(CH3)-}$ groups join through their C2 atoms: $\ce{CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH(CH3)CH2CH3}$. The longest chain has six carbons with methyl groups on C3 and C4 — option (c). Octane (a) would need 1-bromobutane.

questions.stem_md: Sodium butanoate is heated strongly with soda lime (NaOH and CaO). The hydrocarbon formed is:
questions.solution_md: Decarboxylation removes the carboxylate carbon as carbonate: $\ce{CH3CH2CH2COONa + NaOH -> CH3CH2CH3 + Na2CO3}$. The alkane has one carbon less than the salt, so propane — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the conformations of ethane is correct?

options.text_md: The eclipsed form has the lower energy because the hydrogen atoms are closest together.
The staggered form has the lower energy because the C–H bonds of the two carbons are as far apart as possible.
The two forms have the same energy, since the C–C bond is a single bond.
The staggered form has a dihedral angle of 0°.

questions.solution_md: In the staggered form the bonding electron pairs of the two carbons are farthest apart, so torsional strain is minimal; the eclipsed form is about 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹ higher — option (b). The dihedral angle of the staggered form is 60° (d is wrong).

questions.stem_md: n-Heptane is passed over a Cr₂O₃-based catalyst at 773 K and high pressure. The aromatic hydrocarbon formed is:
questions.solution_md: Cyclisation and dehydrogenation: $\ce{C7H16 -> C7H8 + 4H2}$, with seven carbons retained as a methyl-substituted ring — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the staggered conformation of ethane, the dihedral angle between a hydrogen on the front carbon and the nearest hydrogen on the back carbon is:
questions.solution_md: The three hydrogens on each carbon are 120° apart, and in the staggered form each back hydrogen lies midway between two front hydrogens, so the angle is 60° — option (c). 0° is the eclipsed form.

questions.stem_md: In the chlorination of ethane in sunlight, which of these is a chain-propagation step?
questions.solution_md: A propagation step consumes one radical and forms another, so the chain continues: the ethyl radical reacts with Cl₂ to give the product and a new Cl• — option (b). (a) is initiation; (c) and (d) are termination steps in which two radicals disappear.

questions.stem_md: Which of these alkenes can exist as cis and trans isomers?
questions.solution_md: Each carbon of the double bond must carry two different groups. In pent-2-ene, C2 has H and CH₃ and C3 has H and C₂H₅ — option (d). In the others one double-bond carbon has two identical groups (H, H or CH₃, CH₃).

questions.stem_md: Hex-3-yne is treated with sodium in liquid ammonia. The main product is:
questions.solution_md: Sodium in liquid ammonia reduces an internal alkyne to the trans alkene, while hydrogen with Lindlar catalyst gives the cis alkene — option (b). Hexane (c) needs H₂/Ni.

questions.stem_md: 2-Methylbut-2-ene, $\ce{(CH3)2C=CHCH3}$, reacts with HI. The major product is:
questions.solution_md: By Markovnikov’s rule, H adds to the carbon with one hydrogen (C3) and I to C2, the carbon with none. The intermediate is a tertiary carbocation, which gives 2-iodo-2-methylbutane — option (b).

questions.stem_md: 3-Methylbut-1-ene, $\ce{(CH3)2CHCH=CH2}$, is treated with HBr in the presence of benzoyl peroxide. The main product is:
questions.solution_md: With peroxide, HBr adds through bromine radicals: Br• attacks the terminal carbon to give the more stable secondary radical, so bromine ends up on C1 — option (b). Without peroxide the product would be 2-bromo-3-methylbutane (a) or its rearranged isomer (c).

questions.stem_md: An alkene gives only propanone and methanal when it is treated with ozone and then with zinc and water. The alkene is:
questions.solution_md: Join the carbonyl carbons and remove the oxygens: $\ce{(CH3)2C=CH2}$, formula $\ce{C4H8}$ (3 + 1 carbons) — option (a). But-2-ene (c) gives two ethanal.

questions.stem_md: Cold, dilute, alkaline potassium permanganate is added to a liquid hydrocarbon X. The purple colour disappears and a brown precipitate forms. X could be:
questions.solution_md: Alkenes are oxidised to vicinal diols (Baeyer’s test) while MnO₄⁻ is reduced to brown MnO₂ — option (c). Alkanes and benzene do not react in the cold.

questions.stem_md: Which carbocation is the most stable?
questions.solution_md: Three alkyl groups donate electron density (inductive effect and hyperconjugation) and spread the charge, so the tertiary carbocation is the most stable — option (c). The order is 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl.

questions.stem_md: In propyne, CH₃–C≡C–H, the hybridisation of the three carbon atoms, starting from the methyl carbon, is:
questions.solution_md: The methyl carbon has four σ bonds (sp³); each triple-bond carbon has two σ bonds and two π bonds (sp) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Excess hydrogen bromide is passed into but-1-yne. The product is:
questions.solution_md: Each addition follows Markovnikov’s rule, so both bromine atoms end on C2: $\ce{CH#CCH2CH3 + 2HBr -> CH3CBr2CH2CH3}$ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: But-1-yne is shaken with dilute sulfuric acid containing mercury(II) sulfate. The final product is:
questions.solution_md: Water adds by Markovnikov’s rule to give the enol CH₂=C(OH)CH₂CH₃, which rearranges (tautomerism) to the ketone butan-2-one — option (d). Only ethyne gives an aldehyde.

questions.stem_md: Which of these hydrocarbons liberates hydrogen gas when sodium metal is added?
questions.solution_md: Only a terminal alkyne has a hydrogen on an sp carbon acidic enough to be replaced by sodium: $\ce{2C3H7C#CH + 2Na -> 2C3H7C#CNa + H2}$ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In benzene all carbon–carbon bonds are 139 pm long, between the C–C (154 pm) and C=C (134 pm) values. This is because:

options.text_md: the six π electrons are delocalised over the ring, so every bond has partial double-bond character
the ring changes rapidly between single and double bonds
the carbon atoms are sp³ hybridised
three bonds are single and three are double, giving an average

questions.solution_md: Sideways overlap of six p orbitals spreads the π electrons over all six bonds, so they are identical and intermediate in length — option (a). Benzene is a resonance hybrid, not a rapidly flipping pair of structures (b).

questions.stem_md: Benzene is treated with propanoyl chloride, CH₃CH₂COCl, in the presence of anhydrous aluminium chloride. The product is:
questions.solution_md: Friedel–Crafts acylation replaces H by the acyl group: $\ce{C6H6 + CH3CH2COCl -> C6H5COCH2CH3 + HCl}$, an aryl ketone — option (c). The alkylbenzenes (a, b) would need an alkyl halide.

questions.stem_md: In the nitration of benzene with concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid, the attacking electrophile is:
questions.solution_md: Sulfuric acid protonates nitric acid, which loses water: $\ce{HNO3 + 2H2SO4 -> NO2^+ + H3O^+ + 2HSO4^-}$. The electron-poor NO₂⁺ is attacked by the π cloud — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which of these is a carcinogenic polynuclear hydrocarbon formed in the incomplete combustion of coal, petroleum and tobacco?
questions.solution_md: Benzpyrene, with five fused rings, is converted in the body into products that damage DNA — option (d). Naphthalene has only two rings and is not classed as a carcinogen at this level.

questions.stem_md: Which of these compounds is aromatic?

options.text_md: anthracene (14 π electrons, planar, fully conjugated)

questions.solution_md: Anthracene is planar, cyclic and fully conjugated with 14 π electrons, and $14 = 4 \times 3 + 2$, so it obeys the Hückel rule — option (a). 4 and 8 are of the form 4n, and cyclohexene is not conjugated.

questions.stem_md: Benzonitrile, C₆H₅CN, is treated with bromine and iron(III) bromide. The main product is:
questions.solution_md: The –CN group withdraws electrons and deactivates the ring, directing the electrophile to the meta position: 3-bromobenzonitrile — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In the presence of a peroxide, HBr adds to but-1-ene to give 1-bromobutane, but HCl does not show this behaviour.

**Reason (R):** In the radical chain, both propagation steps are energetically favourable for HBr but not for HCl.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. For HCl the strong H–Cl bond makes hydrogen abstraction by the alkyl radical unfavourable, so the chain breaks down; R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** At room temperature the CH₃ groups of ethane rotate almost freely about the C–C bond.

**Reason (R):** The staggered conformation of ethane is more stable than the eclipsed conformation.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but R does not explain A. The free rotation arises because the barrier (about 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹) is small compared with the energy available in collisions at room temperature — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Ethyne reacts with sodium metal to liberate hydrogen gas.

**Reason (R):** Ethyne is a weaker acid than ethene.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the sp C–H of ethyne is acidic enough for sodium to replace H. R is false: the sp carbon (50% s-character) makes ethyne a stronger acid than ethene — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Benzene readily undergoes addition reactions with bromine water, like cyclohexene.

**Reason (R):** Benzene has a delocalised π electron cloud that gives it extra stability.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: benzene does not decolourise bromine water, since addition would destroy its delocalisation energy. R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Nitrobenzene does not undergo Friedel–Crafts alkylation.

**Reason (R):** The nitro group strongly deactivates the benzene ring towards attack by electrophiles.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. The ring is too electron-poor to attack the carbocation, so the reaction fails; R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** trans-But-2-ene has a higher melting point than cis-but-2-ene.

**Reason (R):** trans-But-2-ene is more polar than cis-but-2-ene.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true (168 K against 134 K) because the symmetrical trans molecules pack better in the crystal. R is false: the bond dipoles cancel in the trans isomer, which is the less polar one — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Propene and cyclopropane are isomers of each other.
questions.solution_md: True. Both have the molecular formula $\ce{C3H6}$ but different structures (open chain with C=C, and a ring).

questions.stem_md: True or false? But-1-ene shows cis–trans isomerism.
questions.solution_md: False. In $\ce{CH2=CHCH2CH3}$ the terminal carbon carries two identical hydrogen atoms, so no geometric isomers exist.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Cyclobutadiene, C₄H₄, is aromatic because it is planar, cyclic and fully conjugated.
questions.solution_md: False. It has 4 π electrons, which does not fit the 4n + 2 rule, so it is not aromatic (it is highly unstable).

questions.stem_md: The Wurtz reaction uses sodium metal in dry ___ as the solvent.
questions.solution_md: Dry **ether** (diethyl ether); water would destroy sodium.

questions.stem_md: A terminal alkyne gives a white precipitate of silver ___ with ammoniacal silver nitrate.
questions.solution_md: The precipitate is the silver **alkynide** (acetylide), formed because the terminal ≡C–H is acidic.

questions.stem_md: Lindlar catalyst is palladium on calcium carbonate poisoned with ___.
questions.solution_md: It is poisoned with **quinoline** (or sulfur compounds), so hydrogenation of an alkyne stops at the cis alkene.

questions.stem_md: Match each conversion in Column I with its reagent or condition in Column II.

match_right.text_md: H₂ over Pd/CaCO₃ poisoned with quinoline

questions.solution_md: Lindlar catalyst gives cis; Na/liquid NH₃ gives trans; hydration with Hg²⁺/H⁺ gives ethanal; cyclic polymerisation in a red-hot iron tube gives benzene.

questions.stem_md: Match each substituent on a benzene ring with its effect in electrophilic substitution.

match_right.text_md: Weakly activating, ortho and para directing
Strongly activating, ortho and para directing

questions.solution_md: –OH donates a lone pair (+M) strongly; –CH₃ donates weakly (+I, hyperconjugation); halogens withdraw by –I but direct o/p through +M; –CN withdraws (–M, –I) and directs meta.

questions.stem_md: An open-chain saturated hydrocarbon has a molar mass of 86 g mol⁻¹ (C = 12, H = 1). How many carbon atoms does a molecule contain?
questions.solution_md: For an alkane, $M = 12n + (2n + 2) = 14n + 2 = 86$, so $14n = 84$ and $n = 6$. The hydrocarbon is hexane (or an isomer).

questions.stem_md: A sample of 7.2 g of 2,2-dimethylpropane is burned completely in excess oxygen. What mass of carbon dioxide is formed, in grams? (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
questions.solution_md: $\ce{C5H12 + 8O2 -> 5CO2 + 6H2O}$. $M(\ce{C5H12}) = 5 \times 12 + 12 \times 1 = 72$, so $n = 7.2 \div 72 = 0.10$ mol. Moles of $\ce{CO2} = 5 \times 0.10 = 0.50$, and mass $= 0.50 \times 44 = 22$ g.

marking_scheme.step: Balanced equation and moles of alkane
5 mol CO₂ per mol and mass 22 g

questions.stem_md: The torsional barrier of ethane is 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹. Treating one eclipsed and one staggered conformation as the only two states (ignore entropy differences), calculate how many molecules are eclipsed for every 1000 that are staggered at 298 K. (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
questions.solution_md: Ratio $= e^{-\Delta E/RT}$. $RT = 8.314 \times 298 \approx 2478\ \text{J mol}^{-1}$, so $\Delta E / RT = 12500 \div 2478 \approx 5.05$ and the ratio is $e^{-5.05} \approx 0.0064$. Per 1000 staggered: $1000 \times 0.0064 = 6.4$.

questions.stem_md: The enthalpy of hydrogenation of cyclohexene is −119.5 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of benzene to cyclohexane is −208.4 kJ mol⁻¹ (given). Calculate the resonance energy of benzene, in kJ mol⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: Three isolated C=C bonds would release $3 \times 119.5 = 358.5$ kJ mol⁻¹. Observed: 208.4. Resonance energy $= 358.5 - 208.4 = 150.1$ kJ mol⁻¹.

marking_scheme.step: Expected value for three double bonds

questions.stem_md: Chlorination of 2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CH, in light gives (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Cl and (CH₃)₃CCl. If a tertiary hydrogen is 5.0 times as reactive as a primary hydrogen (given), what percentage of the monochloro product is (CH₃)₃CCl?
questions.solution_md: There are $9$ primary and $1$ tertiary hydrogens. Relative amounts: primary $= 9 \times 1 = 9$, tertiary $= 1 \times 5 = 5$. Percentage of tertiary chloride $= 5 \div (9 + 5) \times 100 = 35.7$.

marking_scheme.step: Counts 9 primary and 1 tertiary H, weighted 9 : 5

questions.stem_md: An alkene of molecular formula C₆H₁₂ gives only propanone on ozonolysis (Zn, H₂O). What mass of propanone, in grams, is obtained from 4.2 g of the alkene? (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
questions.solution_md: The alkene is $\ce{(CH3)2C=C(CH3)2}$, which splits into two propanone molecules. $M(\ce{C6H12}) = 6 \times 12 + 12 = 84$, so $n = 4.2 \div 84 = 0.050$ mol, giving $2 \times 0.050 = 0.10$ mol of propanone. $M(\ce{C3H6O}) = 58$, so mass $= 0.10 \times 58 = 5.8$ g.

marking_scheme.step: Identifies the symmetrical alkene and 2 mol per mol

questions.stem_md: Calcium carbide (3.2 g) reacts completely with excess water, $\ce{CaC2 + 2H2O -> C2H2 + Ca(OH)2}$. What volume of ethyne is obtained at STP, in dm³? (Ca = 40, C = 12; molar volume at STP = 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹)
questions.solution_md: $M(\ce{CaC2}) = 40 + 2 \times 12 = 64$, so $n = 3.2 \div 64 = 0.050$ mol. The ratio is 1 : 1, so $0.050$ mol of ethyne, with volume $0.050 \times 22.4 = 1.12$ dm³.

marking_scheme.step: Moles of CaC₂ = moles of C₂H₂

questions.stem_md: A mixture of bromomethane and 2-bromopropane is warmed with sodium in dry ether. Name all the alkanes that can form, and say why the Wurtz reaction is unsuitable for making an unsymmetrical alkane.

answer.model_answer_md: Three alkanes form: ethane (methyl with methyl), 2-methylpropane (methyl with isopropyl) and 2,3-dimethylbutane (isopropyl with isopropyl). Coupling occurs between like and unlike groups at random, so the mixture is difficult to separate and the yield of the unsymmetrical alkane is low.

questions.solution_md: Three coupling combinations; poor selectivity.

marking_scheme.step: Mixture, hard to separate, low yield

questions.stem_md: How would you convert hex-3-yne into (i) cis-hex-3-ene and (ii) trans-hex-3-ene? Name the reagent in each case.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) Hydrogen over Lindlar catalyst, palladium on calcium carbonate poisoned with quinoline: both hydrogens add to the same face of the triple bond on the catalyst surface, giving the cis alkene and stopping before the alkane. (ii) Sodium in liquid ammonia: the trans alkene is formed.

questions.solution_md: Lindlar gives cis; Na/NH₃ gives trans.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Na in liquid NH₃ and trans product

questions.stem_md: Write the equation for the electrolysis of aqueous potassium propanoate and name the products formed at the anode and at the cathode.

answer.model_answer_md: $\ce{2C2H5COOK + 2H2O -> C4H10 + 2CO2 + H2 + 2KOH}$. At the anode, the propanoate ions lose electrons to give butane and carbon dioxide. At the cathode, water is reduced to hydrogen gas, leaving potassium hydroxide in solution.

questions.solution_md: Kolbe electrolysis joins two ethyl groups.

questions.stem_md: cis-1,2-Dichloroethene boils at about 333 K and the trans isomer at about 321 K. Explain the difference.

answer.model_answer_md: In the cis isomer the two C–Cl bond dipoles point to the same side and add up, so the molecule is polar and has dipole–dipole attractions as well as dispersion forces. In the trans isomer the dipoles cancel and the molecule is non-polar, so the forces are weaker and it boils lower.

questions.solution_md: Polarity decides the boiling point.

marking_scheme.step: Dipoles add in cis, cancel in trans

questions.stem_md: Explain why the peroxide effect is observed with HBr but not with HCl or HI.

answer.model_answer_md: In the radical chain, the carbon radical must remove a hydrogen from HX. For HCl the H–Cl bond is so strong that this step is unfavourable, and for HI the iodine atom adds to the alkene too slowly and simply pairs up to give I₂. Only HBr has both propagation steps favourable.

questions.solution_md: Only HBr suits both chain steps.

marking_scheme.step: HCl: strong H–Cl bond, hydrogen abstraction unfavourable
HI: iodine atoms too unreactive; HBr suits both steps

questions.stem_md: Explain why ethyne reacts with sodium amide whereas ethene does not.

answer.model_answer_md: The carbons of ethyne are sp hybridised with 50 percent s-character, so they hold electrons nearer the nucleus and are more electronegative than the sp² carbons of ethene (33 percent). The ≡C–H hydrogen is therefore acidic and is removed by the strong base: $\ce{CH#CH + NaNH2 -> CH#CNa + NH3}$.

questions.solution_md: sp carbon stabilises the carbanion.

marking_scheme.step: Higher s-character of sp carbon makes ≡C–H acidic

questions.stem_md: Benzene is drawn with three C=C bonds, yet it undergoes substitution rather than addition. Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: The six π electrons are delocalised over the whole ring, which gives benzene about 150 kJ per mole of extra stability. Addition reactions would destroy this delocalisation, whereas substitution keeps the aromatic ring intact, so benzene prefers electrophilic substitution to addition.

questions.solution_md: Resonance stabilisation is retained in substitution.

marking_scheme.step: Substitution retains the ring, addition destroys it

questions.stem_md: Apply the Hückel rule to benzene, naphthalene and cyclooctatetraene, and state which are aromatic.

answer.model_answer_md: A ring is aromatic if it is planar, cyclic, fully conjugated and has 4n + 2 π electrons. Benzene has 6 electrons (n = 1) and naphthalene has 10 (n = 2); both are planar and conjugated, so both are aromatic. Cyclooctatetraene has 8 π electrons, which is 4n and not 4n + 2, and it is tub-shaped rather than planar, so it is not aromatic.

questions.solution_md: Count π electrons and test 4n + 2.

marking_scheme.step: Statement of the rule with its conditions
Benzene and naphthalene aromatic with n values

questions.stem_md: Write the structures and IUPAC names of all the chain isomers of C₅H₁₂. Which has the lowest boiling point, and why?

answer.model_answer_md: Pentane, $\ce{CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3}$; 2-methylbutane, $\ce{(CH3)2CHCH2CH3}$; and 2,2-dimethylpropane, $\ce{C(CH3)4}$. These are the only three arrangements of five carbon atoms in a chain. The last, the most branched, boils lowest (about 283 K) because its molecules are almost spherical, with the smallest surface area of contact and the weakest van der Waals forces.

questions.solution_md: Three isomers; branching lowers the boiling point.

marking_scheme.step: Lowest boiling point identified with reason

questions.stem_md: (a) An alkene A, C₅H₁₀, gives ethanal and propanal on ozonolysis with Zn and water. Identify A. (b) Predict the products of ozonolysis of 2-methylbut-2-ene.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Ozonolysis turns each carbon of the double bond into a carbonyl carbon, so to find A we join the two carbonyl carbons by a double bond and remove the oxygens: $\ce{CH3CH=CHCH2CH3}$, pent-2-ene. (b) The alkene $\ce{(CH3)2C=CHCH3}$ is cut at the double bond; the $\ce{(CH3)2C=}$ end gives propanone and the $\ce{=CHCH3}$ end gives ethanal.

questions.solution_md: Work forwards or backwards across the C=C bond.

questions.stem_md: Classify –OH, –Cl and –NO₂ as activating or deactivating and as ortho/para or meta directing. Why does –NO₂ direct meta?

answer.model_answer_md: –OH is activating and ortho/para directing; –Cl is deactivating but ortho/para directing; –NO₂ is deactivating and meta directing. The nitro group withdraws electrons by its –M and –I effects, and this removes more electron density from the ortho and para positions than from the meta position, so the electrophile attacks meta, the least deactivated site.

questions.solution_md: Electron withdrawal is felt most at o and p.

questions.stem_md: Describe the three stages of the free-radical monochlorination of methane in sunlight, with an equation for each.

answer.model_answer_md: Initiation: light splits a chlorine molecule, Cl₂ → 2Cl•. Propagation: Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + CH₃•, then CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•, so the chain repeats. Termination: two radicals combine, for example Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂, CH₃• + CH₃• → C₂H₆ or CH₃• + Cl• → CH₃Cl, which ends the chain.

questions.solution_md: Initiation, propagation, termination.

questions.stem_md: What are polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons? Give one example, say how it is formed, and explain why it is dangerous.

answer.model_answer_md: Polynuclear hydrocarbons contain three or more benzene rings fused together. Benzpyrene is an example. It forms when coal, petroleum, wood or tobacco burn incompletely. Entering the body, it undergoes biochemical reactions that give products which damage DNA and can cause cancer, so such compounds are carcinogenic.

questions.solution_md: Fused rings; incomplete combustion; DNA damage.

questions.stem_md: (a) Describe the preparation of ethane by (i) the Wurtz reaction, (ii) decarboxylation and (iii) Kolbe electrolysis, giving equations. (b) Describe the mechanism of the monochlorination of methane in sunlight.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) (i) Bromomethane with sodium in dry ether: $\ce{2CH3Br + 2Na -> C2H6 + 2NaBr}$. (ii) Sodium propanoate heated with soda lime loses one carbon: $\ce{CH3CH2COONa + NaOH -> CH3CH3 + Na2CO3}$. questions.stem_md: (a) Explain the structure of benzene in terms of resonance and its π cloud. (b) Write the mechanism of the nitration of benzene, showing how the electrophile is produced.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Benzene is a planar hexagon with all C–C bonds 139 pm, between a single and a double bond. It is a resonance hybrid of two Kekulé structures; each carbon is sp² and the six p orbitals overlap sideways, so six π electrons are delocalised above and below the ring. (b) Nitric acid and sulfuric acid form the nitronium ion: $\ce{HNO3 + 2H2SO4 -> NO2^+ + H3O^+ + 2HSO4^-}$. The π cloud attacks NO₂⁺ in the slow step to give the arenium ion, in which the charge is spread over the ring. Loss of H⁺ restores aromaticity and gives nitrobenzene.

questions.stem_md: (a) State Markovnikov’s rule and explain it with the mechanism of the addition of HBr to propene. (b) Explain how the product of the addition of HBr to but-1-ene changes in the presence of a peroxide, and give the mechanism.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) In the addition of HX to an unsymmetrical alkene, hydrogen goes to the carbon with more hydrogens. The π bond attacks H⁺ to give the more stable secondary carbocation $\ce{CH3CH^+CH3}$, which bromide traps to give 2-bromopropane. (b) With peroxide, Br• radicals form: ROOR gives RO•, which takes H from HBr. Br• adds to the terminal carbon, giving the more stable secondary radical; this takes H from HBr, giving 1-bromobutane and a new Br•, so the chain continues. The product is anti-Markovnikov.
